**This vehicle answered one question and its first flight was destroyed by another, and both
questions were the same question.** A scramjet's useful output is the difference between the thrust it
makes and the drag it suffers, and each of those is far larger than the difference. A launch vehicle's
stability is the difference between the gain its control loop has and the gain at which it goes
unstable, and each of those is far larger than the difference. **The Hyper-X programme measured the
first correctly and got the second wrong**, and this article treats the two as a single subject.
This is the forty-fourth article in the [X-Planes series][related_post_a297_framing], following the [X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1], the [X-2][related_post_a299_bell_x2], the [X-3][related_post_a300_douglas_x3], the [X-4][related_post_a301_northrop_x4], the [X-5][related_post_a302_bell_x5], the [X-6][related_post_a303_convair_x6], the [X-7][related_post_a304_lockheed_x7], the [X-8][related_post_a305_aerojet_x8], the [X-9][related_post_a306_bell_x9], the [X-10][related_post_a307_north_american_x10], the [X-11][related_post_a308_convair_x11], the [X-12][related_post_a309_convair_x12], the [X-13][related_post_a310_ryan_x13], the [X-14][related_post_a311_bell_x14], the [X-15][related_post_a312_north_american_x15], the [X-16][related_post_a313_bell_x16], the [X-17][related_post_a314_lockheed_x17], the [X-18][related_post_a315_hiller_x18], the [X-19][related_post_a316_curtiss_wright_x19], the [X-20][related_post_a317_boeing_x20], the [X-21][related_post_a318_northrop_x21], the [X-22][related_post_a319_bell_x22], the [X-23][related_post_a320_martin_marietta_x23], the [X-24][related_post_a321_martin_marietta_x24], the [X-25][related_post_a322_bensen_x25], the [X-26][related_post_a323_schweizer_x26], the [X-27][related_post_a324_lockheed_x27], the [X-28][related_post_a325_osprey_x28], the [X-29][related_post_a326_grumman_x29], the [X-30][related_post_a327_rockwell_x30], the [X-31][related_post_a328_rockwell_mbb_x31], the [X-32][related_post_a329_boeing_x32], the [X-33][related_post_a330_lockheed_martin_x33], the [X-34][related_post_a331_orbital_sciences_x34], the [X-35][related_post_a332_lockheed_martin_x35], the [X-36][related_post_a333_mcdonnell_douglas_x36], the [X-37][related_post_a334_boeing_x37], the [X-38][related_post_a335_scaled_composites_x38], the [X-39][related_post_a336_x39_reserved_never_assigned], the [X-40][related_post_a337_boeing_x40], the [X-41][related_post_a338_x41_common_aero_vehicle], and the [X-42][related_post_a339_orbital_sciences_x42].

**The Hyper-X programme left an extensive public record.** The
programme was a joint one of the Langley and Dryden centres of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, NASA\[[Rausch et al. 2000][research_rausch_2000]\], and it published extensively, including the design,
the ground test campaign and the flight results at Mach 7\[[Ferlemann et al. 2005][research_ferlemann_2005]\], the Mach 10 flight\[[Marshall et al. 2005b][research_marshall_2005]\], and a mishap investigation board
report of unusual candour\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\]. **With this much primary material, the question is which documents
matter**, and the source base below names them.

## The Research Question

**The binding unknown was whether an airframe-integrated scramjet could produce more thrust than the
vehicle carrying it produced drag, in free flight, at hypersonic speed.**

Supersonic combustion had been demonstrated in ground facilities since the 1960s, and scramjet
flowpaths had been run in shock tunnels and combustion-heated tunnels for
decades\[[Guy 1990][research_guy_1990]\]\[[Drummond 1991b][research_drummond_1991]\].
**None of that settles the question**, for a reason unrelated to the accuracy of ground facilities. The
quantity in question is not a property of the engine.

**A scramjet is not installed in an airframe. It is the airframe.** The forebody is the first stage of
the inlet, the underside is the flowpath, and the afterbody is the
nozzle\[[Heiser and Pratt][book_heiser_pratt]\]\[[Engelund et al. 1999][research_engelund_1999]\]. There is no station at which
one can put a thrust stand and no surface across which thrust and drag are separable in principle.
**What the vehicle produces is a single net axial force**, and the design question is whether that
force has the sign the designer intended.

$$F_{\text{net}} = F_{\text{thrust}} - D$$

**That equation is trivial, and it contains the whole problem.** Writing out the thrust term shows why.
Uninstalled thrust is a momentum difference plus a pressure term,

$$F_{\text{thrust}} = \dot{m}_{e} V_{e} - \dot{m}_{0} V_{0} + \left( p_{e} - p_{0} \right) A_{e}$$

and the captured air flow is

$$\dot{m}_{0} = \rho V_{0} A_{c}$$

**For a hydrogen scramjet at stoichiometric the fuel flow is about 2.9 percent of the air flow.** Two
moles of hydrogen burn each mole of oxygen, and air carries oxygen at a mole fraction $x_{\mathrm{O_2}}$
of 0.209476 and a mean molar mass $\mathcal{M}_{\text{air}}$ of 28.9644 grams per mole in the 1976
standard atmosphere\[[U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 1976][research_us_atmos_1976]\], so the stoichiometric
fuel to air mass ratio is

$$f_{\text{st}} = \frac{2 \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{H_2}} \, x_{\mathrm{O_2}}}{\mathcal{M}_{\text{air}}} = \frac{2 \times 2.016 \times 0.209476}{28.9644} = 0.0292$$

with $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{H_2}}$ the molar mass of hydrogen. The two mass flows are therefore nearly
equal and the thrust is dominated by the velocity difference,

$$F_{\text{thrust}} \approx \dot{m}_{0} \left( V_{e} - V_{0} \right)$$

**The exit velocity exceeds the flight velocity by a few percent, not by a factor.** Taking a five
percent excess as an illustration, the thrust per unit of captured air flow is

$$\frac{F_{\text{thrust}}}{\dot{m}_{0}} = 0.05 \, V_{0} = 0.05 \times 2{,}056 = 103 \ \tfrac{\text{N}}{\text{kg/s}} \qquad 0.05 \times 2{,}959 = 148 \ \tfrac{\text{N}}{\text{kg/s}}$$

at the Mach 6.83 and Mach 9.68 flight speeds derived below. **Everything in the engine is spent on that few percent**, and the drag
is subtracted from it afterwards. At the flight condition, both terms are large
and their difference is small. A ground facility can produce one of them with an uncertainty band, and
computational fluid dynamics can produce the other with an uncertainty band, and if those bands are
comparable to the difference then no combination of ground testing and analysis can tell you the sign
of the answer. **Only the vehicle can, by accelerating or failing to.**

**The programme knew this and said so in its objectives.** The stated primary goal was not to fly fast.
It was to demonstrate and flight validate the analytical design tools, computational methods and
experimental techniques required to develop a hypersonic air-breathing
aircraft\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\]. **The product of Hyper-X was
meant to be calibrated tools**, and the vehicle was the calibration article.

## Programme Origin

**NASA initiated Hyper-X in 1996 as an explicitly high-risk, high-payoff
programme**\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\], and its immediate ancestor
is the failure of something much larger.

The National Aero-Space Plane had proposed a single-stage air-breathing vehicle flying from a runway to
orbit\[[Piland 1987][research_piland_1987]\]\[[Tank 1991][research_tank_1991]\]. NASA's history of the
X-43A records that it received government approval in 1986 and was cancelled in October 1994, after some
2.4 billion dollars and eight years of work, without a workable design and without a flight
article\[[Peebles 2007][research_peebles_2007]\]. **The propulsion state of
the art it left behind was surveyed at the time**, and the survey makes plain that the hard part was
never the combustion but the
integration\[[Guy 1990][research_guy_1990]\]. **Hyper-X inverted its logic.** The earlier programme had designed an operational
vehicle around propulsion that had never flown. Hyper-X proposed to fly the propulsion first, on a vehicle
small enough to be expendable, and to use the resulting data to calibrate the tools that any later
vehicle would be designed with.

**The concept came out of the panels that reviewed the end of that programme.** The programme's
technology summary records that NASA developed Hyper-X in 1995 and 1996 after several blue-ribbon
panels recommended flight experiments with airframe-integrated scramjets as the next major step in
hypersonic research\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\]. **The first public description
planned four flights on four expendable twelve foot vehicles**, a Mach 7 flight first, scheduled for
the middle of 1999, then Mach 5, then two at Mach 10\[[Freeman et al. 1997][research_freeman_1997]\].
The first flight was in fact made in June 2001\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\]. **Cost growth during design
restructured the project**, and the Mach 5 flight was dropped in favour of two flights at Mach 7 and
one at Mach 10\[[Peebles 2007][research_peebles_2007]\].

**The programme was a collaboration between Langley Research Center and Dryden Flight Research
Center**\[[Rausch et al. 2000][research_rausch_2000]\]\[[McClinton et al. 2001][research_mcclinton_2001]\],
with shared responsibility for mission success. Langley was responsible for hypersonic technology
development, including many of the critical vehicle design and risk reduction activities. Dryden was
responsible for vehicle development, including booster integration, system validation and flight
testing\[[McClinton et al. 2001][research_mcclinton_2001]\]. **Two industrial
contracts split the flight hardware**, with Micro Craft responsible for the Hyper-X Research Vehicle
and its adapter, and Orbital Sciences Corporation responsible for the Hyper-X Launch
Vehicle\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].

**Three flights were planned and each research vehicle was non-recoverable**\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\]. Non-recoverability was a design
decision, and its consequences run through the rest of this article. A vehicle that will be destroyed on every mission
cannot be instrumented for post-flight inspection, so every measurement must be telemetered in real
time, and any measurement not taken during the ten seconds of powered flight is not taken at all.

**The programme is unusual in this series for having published its own failure in detail**, and one of
its chief engineers later published a personal account of the flight test
as well\[[Marshall et al. 2005a][research_marshall_corpening_2005]\]. The mishap
investigation board convened on 5 June 2001, three days after the first flight, and its report of
findings runs to five volumes, of which the first is public, with its sections on findings and
recommendations withheld as export controlled\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].
**It is the best single source on this vehicle** and it
is used throughout this article, including for the vehicle description, because the board had to
establish the configuration before it could analyse the loss.

## Sizing From First Principles

**One number explains why this vehicle exists, the temperature of the air after it has been slowed down.**

### Why the Combustion Has to Be Supersonic

**The compressible flow relations this article uses are all standard and all come from one place.**
Report 1135 of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics, the body NASA replaced in 1958,
tabulates the isentropic relations, the oblique shock relations and the Rayleigh flow relation in the
forms used below\[[Ames Research Staff 1953][research_naca_1135]\], and the modern
textbook treatments state them
identically\[[Anderson][book_anderson_hypersonic]\]\[[Heiser and Pratt][book_heiser_pratt]\]. **This
article claims no originality in any relation it displays**, only in applying them to a vehicle whose
flight conditions were reported piecemeal.

Air brought to rest from a high Mach number arrives at its stagnation temperature. For a calorically
perfect gas of ratio of specific heats $\gamma$, moving at Mach number $M$ through air at static
temperature $T$,

$$T_{0} = T \left( 1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2} M^{2} \right)$$

**The two powered flights reached Mach 6.83 in nearly level flight at about 95,000 feet and Mach 9.68
at about 110,000 feet**, the maximum powered Mach numbers the flight reports give\[[Marshall et al. 2005a][research_marshall_corpening_2005]\]\[[Marshall et al. 2005b][research_marshall_2005]\]\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\].
Taking the static temperature at each altitude from the 1976 standard atmosphere, 225.5 and 232.4
kelvin\[[U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 1976][research_us_atmos_1976]\], the relation evaluates to

$$T_{0} = 225.5 \left( 1 + 0.2 \times 6.83^{2} \right) = 2{,}329 \ \text{K}$$

$$T_{0} = 232.4 \left( 1 + 0.2 \times 9.68^{2} \right) = 4{,}588 \ \text{K}$$

**A ramjet works by decelerating the flow to subsonic speed before burning it.** If this vehicle's
inlet had done that, taking the flow only as far as sonic conditions, the static temperature entering
the combustor would be

$$T_{\text{throat}} = \frac{T_{0}}{1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2}} = \frac{T_{0}}{1.2}$$

which is 1,941 kelvin at Mach 6.83 and 3,824 kelvin at Mach 9.68.

**Oxygen begins to dissociate appreciably above roughly 2,500 kelvin and nitrogen above roughly 4,000
kelvin**\[[Anderson][book_anderson_hypersonic]\]. At the Mach 10 condition, a subsonic-combustion inlet delivers air to the combustor that is
already coming apart, before any fuel has been added. **The energy spent breaking those molecules is
energy unavailable to push the vehicle**, and the nozzle does not recover it because recombination
is too slow at the residence times involved.

**On the pressure side, the same relation identifies the inlet as the hard part.** The total pressure
ratio available at those conditions is

$$\frac{p_{0}}{p} = \left( 1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2} M^{2} \right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma - 1}}$$

which is 3,543 at Mach 6.83 and 34,178 at Mach 9.68. **A perfect inlet would
deliver all of it and a real one loses total pressure across every shock**, with the losses
compounding, which is why hypersonic compression is taken through several weak oblique shocks rather
than one strong one.

**So the reason for supersonic combustion is not efficiency. It is that the alternative destroys the
working fluid.** A scramjet decelerates the flow only partly, keeping it supersonic through the
combustor, which keeps the static temperature low enough that the air survives to be burned.

### The Trajectory Is a Line of Constant Dynamic Pressure

An air-breathing engine's thrust scales with the mass of air it captures, which scales with density,
while the structural and thermal loads scale with dynamic pressure,

$$q = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^{2}$$

with the flight velocity following from the Mach number and the local speed of sound,

$$V = M a \qquad a = \sqrt{\gamma R T}$$

**A vehicle accelerating through the hypersonic range therefore flies a corridor rather than a
trajectory**, climbing as it accelerates so that the dynamic pressure stays roughly constant. Taking
the 1976 standard atmosphere\[[U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 1976][research_us_atmos_1976]\] at the two flight
altitudes and the two flight Mach numbers gives

| | Mach | Altitude, ft | $\rho$, kg/m³ | $V$, m/s | $q$, lbf/ft² |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flight 2 | 6.83 | 95,000 | 0.0216 | 2,056 | 955 |
| Flight 3 | 9.68 | 110,000 | 0.01065 | 2,959 | 973 |

Worked out at the two conditions,

$$q_{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.0216 \times 2{,}056^{2} = 45.7 \ \text{kPa} = 955 \ \text{lbf/ft}^{2}$$

$$q_{3} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.01065 \times 2{,}959^{2} = 46.6 \ \text{kPa} = 973 \ \text{lbf/ft}^{2}$$

**The design point was a dynamic pressure of about 1,000 pounds per square foot at about 100,000
feet**\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\], and the standard-atmosphere values above
fall within five percent of it at Mach numbers differing by more than forty percent. **The flights
themselves did not hold the same dynamic pressure as closely as the standard atmosphere suggests.**
Voland and his colleagues give the powered portions as about 980 pounds per square foot on
the second flight and about 930 on the third\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\].
For the second flight the programme modelled the atmosphere from sixteen weather balloons launched from
four sites around the range, in order to compute Mach number and dynamic
pressure\[[Karlgaard et al. 2004][research_karlgaard_tartabini_2004]\]. The relative departure
of each standard-atmosphere figure from the reported one is

$$\frac{q_{\text{std}} - q_{\text{rep}}}{q_{\text{rep}}} = \frac{955 - 980}{980} = -2.6 \ \% \qquad \frac{973 - 930}{930} = +4.6 \ \%$$

**So the reported dynamic pressures differ from each other by 50 pounds per square foot, about five
percent, where the standard atmosphere places them within 18 of each other.** Since
$q = \tfrac{1}{2} \gamma p M^{2}$, a departure at a given Mach number is a departure in static
pressure, and it measures how far the day's atmosphere and the altitudes actually flown differ from
the standard. The altitude and Mach pairings are therefore consistent with the design corridor,
and the standard atmosphere is adequate for every order-of-magnitude argument in this article, but it
is not a substitute for the reconstructed flight conditions.

### The Inlet Has a Geometric Limit Nobody Can Design Around

A supersonic inlet that swallows its shock system is said to be started. One that does not is unstarted
and produces drag instead of compression. **The criterion that bounds it was published in 1945 and has
not been improved on as a first estimate**\[[Kantrowitz and Donaldson 1945][research_kantrowitz_1945]\].
**It sets how much contraction a fixed-geometry inlet may have and still start**, by requiring that the flow behind a normal shock at
the capture plane can pass the throat,

$$\frac{A_{\text{throat}}}{A_{\text{capture}}} \geq \frac{1}{A/A^{*} \big|_{M_{2}}} \qquad M_{2}^{2} = \frac{1 + \frac{\gamma-1}{2} M^{2}}{\gamma M^{2} - \frac{\gamma-1}{2}}$$

Evaluated across the range of interest this gives a maximum contraction ratio of 1.60 to 1 at Mach 7
and 1.63 to 1 at Mach 10.

**The useful finding is that the limit barely moves with Mach number.** An inlet sized to start at
the lower end of its range is not penalised much at the upper end, so a fixed-geometry flowpath is
tractable for a vehicle that must work across a range of conditions. **A variable-geometry
inlet buys very little here and costs a great deal.**

### The Closure, and How Small the Answer Is

The vehicle's net axial force produces an acceleration,

$$a = \frac{F_{\text{net}}}{m} = \frac{F_{\text{thrust}} - D}{m}$$

At the research vehicle's mass of about 3,000 pounds\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\], the net force corresponding to a measurable acceleration is small.

| Acceleration | Net axial force, N | Net axial force, lbf |
|---|---|---|
| 0.01 g | 133 | 30 |
| 0.02 g | 267 | 60 |
| 0.05 g | 667 | 150 |

**The entire result of the Mach 7 flight is a net force of that order**, the difference between a
thrust and a drag each of which is far larger. **This is why the question could not be
settled on the ground.** An uncertainty of a few percent on either large quantity swamps the
difference, and a few percent is optimistic for hypersonic force prediction on an integrated
configuration.

## Dependent Systems

### The Airframe Is the Engine

The forebody generates the first compression through a series of oblique shocks before the flow reaches
the cowl\[[Engelund et al. 1999][research_engelund_1999]\]. **Each of those is governed by the same
relation**\[[Ames Research Staff 1953][research_naca_1135]\], which ties the wedge turning angle
$\theta$ to the shock angle $\beta$ at free stream Mach number $M$,

$$\tan \theta = 2 \cot \beta \, \frac{M^{2} \sin^{2} \beta - 1}{M^{2} \left( \gamma + \cos 2 \beta \right) + 2}$$

and the property jumps across the shock follow from the normal component
$M_{n1} = M \sin \beta$,

$$\frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}} = 1 + \frac{2 \gamma}{\gamma + 1} \left( M_{n1}^{2} - 1 \right) \qquad \frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}} = \frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}} \cdot \frac{2 + \left( \gamma - 1 \right) M_{n1}^{2}}{\left( \gamma + 1 \right) M_{n1}^{2}}$$

At the Mach 7 condition, representative turning angles give

| $\beta$, deg | $\theta$, deg | $p_{2}/p_{1}$ | $T_{2}/T_{1}$ | $M_{2}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | 4.97 | 2.19 | 1.27 | 5.98 |
| 15 | 8.38 | 3.48 | 1.51 | 5.41 |
| 20 | 13.37 | 6.20 | 1.98 | 4.59 |

**A single ten degree turn at Mach 7 raises the static pressure more than fourfold and costs nearly
two Mach numbers**, and the forebody stacks several such turns before the cowl. **The vehicle's angle of attack is therefore an engine parameter**, because it sets the
effective wedge angle of the first compression surface and so the capture and the compression ratio.
This coupling is the reason the aerodynamic database and the propulsion database could not be developed
independently, and the programme treated them as one problem from the
start\[[Engelund et al. 1999][research_engelund_1999]\]\[[Engelund et al. 2000][research_engelund_holland_2000]\].

**The wind tunnel programme that supported this was extensive.** Langley ran the vehicle across its
tunnel complex to build a database covering the separation condition, the powered condition and the
descent\[[McClinton et al. 1998a][research_mcclinton_1998]\]\[[Holland et al. 2000][research_holland_2000]\],
and the engine flowpath was run separately in the 8-foot High Temperature Tunnel and in shock
tunnels\[[Huebner et al. 2000][research_huebner_2000]\]\[[Bakos et al. 2001][research_bakos_2001]\].
**The flight engine itself was then ground tested as a risk reduction exercise before each
mission**\[[Huebner et al. 2001][research_huebner_2001]\], a step that distinguishes a flight
programme from a test campaign.

### Isolator, Combustor and the Dual Mode

**Heat cannot be added to a supersonic flow without limit, and the limit is geometric rather than
chemical.** Rayleigh flow, meaning frictionless flow in a constant area duct with heat addition, drives
the Mach number toward unity from either side\[[Ames Research Staff 1953][research_naca_1135]\], and the maximum heat addition is fixed by the ratio of
the stagnation temperature to its value at choking,

$$\frac{T_{0}}{T_{0}^{*}} = \frac{\left( \gamma + 1 \right) M^{2} \left[ 2 + \left( \gamma - 1 \right) M^{2} \right]}{\left( 1 + \gamma M^{2} \right)^{2}}$$

| Combustor entry Mach | $T_{0}/T_{0}^{*}$ | Permissible $T_{0}$ rise |
|---|---|---|
| 1.5 | 0.909 | 10 % |
| 2.0 | 0.793 | 26 % |
| 2.5 | 0.710 | 41 % |
| 3.0 | 0.654 | 53 % |

**A combustor entering at Mach 2 may raise its stagnation temperature by only about a quarter before
it chokes.** The constraint severely limits how much fuel may be burned, and the isolator exists
because of it.

Between the inlet throat and the combustor sits an isolator, a constant or nearly constant
area duct whose job is to contain the shock train that forms when the combustor runs at a pressure the
inlet would not otherwise tolerate\[[Heiser and Pratt][book_heiser_pratt]\]. **Without it, combustor
pressure propagates upstream and unstarts the inlet.** The isolator converts what would be an inlet failure into a shock train that shortens and
lengthens as the fuelling changes.

**The engine was dual mode**, meaning it operated with subsonic combustion at the lower end of its
range and supersonic combustion at the upper end, with the transition managed by fuel
distribution\[[Voland et al. 1998][research_voland_1998]\]\[[Heiser and Pratt][book_heiser_pratt]\]. The isolator matters most in the
subsonic-combustion mode, the condition that drives a shock train upstream.

**The combustor has about a millisecond to work in and often much less.** Taking the combustor
velocity as a fraction of flight velocity and a representative length for a vehicle of this size,

$$t_{\text{res}} = \frac{L_{c}}{V_{c}}$$

gives residence times of roughly 970 microseconds at Mach 6.83 and 680 at Mach 9.68, for a one metre
combustor at half the flight speed. Both are illustrative values assumed here, and neither is a
published dimension of this engine. **At those times the problem is mixing
rather than chemistry**, because turbulent mixing is slower than hydrogen kinetics, and every injector
design is a compromise between fuel penetration and total pressure
loss\[[Drummond 1991b][research_drummond_1991]\].

**Ignition used silane.** A silane and hydrogen mixture, which is pyrophoric and ignites on contact
with air, was used to assure ignition and establish the flame before the engine transitioned to
hydrogen
alone\[[Voland et al. 1998][research_voland_1998]\]\[[Ferlemann et al. 2005][research_ferlemann_2005]\]\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\].

### The Nozzle Is the Back of the Aeroplane

The afterbody is a single expansion ramp, and the exhaust expands against it and against the free
stream on the other side\[[Engelund et al. 2000][research_engelund_holland_2000]\]. **The consequence is that nozzle performance depends on the external flow**,
so thrust varies with angle of attack and with Mach number through a mechanism that has no counterpart
in a conventional engine. **It also means the exhaust contributes a pitching moment**, and the trim
state and the propulsion state are coupled.

### Thermal Protection and the Leading Edges

Stagnation point convective heating scales as

$$\dot{q}_{s} = k \sqrt{\frac{\rho}{R_{n}}} \, V^{3}$$

with $R_{n}$ the leading edge radius. **The correlation is that of Sutton and
Graves**\[[Sutton and Graves 1971][research_sutton_graves_1971]\], which generalises the dissociated-air
stagnation point analysis of Fay and Riddell\[[Fay and Riddell 1958][research_fay_riddell_1958]\] into a
form usable across gas mixtures. **The constant carries the chemistry and the article uses the standard
air value**, so the figures below are estimates from the correlation and are not flow solutions. **The design
radius is documented.** The desired nose tip radius on the Hyper-X vehicles was 0.030
inch\[[Ohlhorst et al. 2005][research_ohlhorst_2005]\], which is 0.762 millimetres, and evaluated
at that radius at the two flight conditions the correlation gives

| | $\rho$, kg/m³ | $V$, m/s | $\dot{q}_{s}$, MW/m² | W/cm² |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flight 2 | 0.0216 | 2,056 | 8.06 | 806 |
| Flight 3 | 0.01065 | 2,959 | 16.86 | 1,686 |

The ratio between the two conditions at equal radius decomposes cleanly,

$$\frac{\dot{q}_{3}}{\dot{q}_{2}} = \left( \frac{V_{3}}{V_{2}} \right)^{3} \sqrt{\frac{\rho_{3}}{\rho_{2}}} = \left( 1.439 \right)^{3} \times \sqrt{0.492} = 2.98 \times 0.702 = 2.09$$

**Mach 9.68 doubles the leading edge heating of Mach 6.83**, at dynamic pressures within five percent of
each other, because the cube of a 1.44 velocity ratio beats the square root of a 0.49 density ratio.

**The programme's own thermal analysis reached the same conclusion and the third vehicle was changed
because of it.** For the Mach 7 vehicles the analysis put the carbon-carbon nose at no more than
3,000 degrees Fahrenheit, so a silicon carbide oxidation coating was adequate, and the four vertical
tail leading edge pieces could be made of a Haynes alloy. For the Mach 10 vehicle at the same 0.030
inch radius it predicted nearly 4,000 degrees Fahrenheit at the nose tip, which no silicon carbide
coating survives even for one short flight. The Mach 10 leading edges were therefore remade in a
high-conductivity carbon-carbon with a hafnium carbide outer coating, the vertical tail leading edges
joined the nose and horizontal tails in that material, and after unexpected erosion in an arc-jet test
the nose was redesigned to a 0.050 inch radius\[[Ohlhorst et al. 2005][research_ohlhorst_2005]\].
The Mach 10 overview confirms the solid Haynes alloy vertical tails and the carbon-carbon tail leading
edges of the third vehicle\[[Marshall et al. 2005b][research_marshall_2005]\]. In kelvin the two
predicted nose temperatures are

$$T_{\text{K}} = \tfrac{5}{9} \left( T_{\text{F}} - 32 \right) + 273.15 \qquad 3{,}000 \ {}^{\circ}\text{F} = 1{,}922 \ \text{K} \qquad 4{,}000 \ {}^{\circ}\text{F} = 2{,}478 \ \text{K}$$

well below the stagnation temperatures of 2,329 and 4,588 kelvin derived above, as they must be for a
nose that conducts heat away and radiates it, and the gap is far wider at Mach 10.

**The blunter nose recovers part of the factor of two.** Heating falls as the square root of the
radius, so the third vehicle's nose at 1.270 millimetres stood against the second vehicle's design
radius in the ratio

$$\frac{\dot{q}_{3}}{\dot{q}_{2}} = 2.09 \times \sqrt{\frac{0.030}{0.050}} = 2.09 \times 0.775 = 1.62$$

which in the correlation is 13.06 megawatts per square metre at the third flight's nose against 8.06
at the second's.

**The relation also explains the shape.** A blunt leading edge is thermally cheap and aerodynamically
expensive, while a sharp one is the reverse. A vehicle whose forebody is an inlet cannot afford a blunt
leading edge, so it pays the heating, and the edges around the nose and wings were
carbon-carbon\[[Marshall et al. 2005a][research_marshall_corpening_2005]\].

### Control, and the Ten Seconds Available

The research vehicle had a flight control system designed for a regime with no flight-validated
aerodynamic model\[[Davidson et al. 1999][research_davidson_1999]\], and its powered mission
lasted about eleven seconds on each flight\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\]. At the
flight speeds that is a short distance,

$$d = V t_{\text{burn}}$$

| | $V$, m/s | $t_{\text{burn}}$, s | $d$, km | $d$, statute miles | Reported, miles |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flight 2 | 2,056 | 11 | 22.6 | 14.1 | 15 |
| Flight 3 | 2,959 | 10.5 | 31.1 | 19.3 | 20 |

The burn times and the reported distances are those of the programme's technology summary, which
records the second vehicle accelerating under its own power for 15 miles in 11 seconds and the third
covering 20 miles in 10.5 seconds of powered flight\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\].
Worked out,

$$d_{2} = 2{,}056 \times 11 = 22.6 \ \text{km} \qquad d_{3} = 2{,}959 \times 10.5 = 31.1 \ \text{km}$$

**The computed distances fall short of the reported ones**, by

$$1 - \frac{22.6}{15 \times 1.609} = 6.3 \ \% \qquad 1 - \frac{31.1}{20 \times 1.609} = 3.5 \ \%$$

and both are larger than rounding to the nearest mile explains, which is 3.3 and 2.5 percent. The reports do not say
whether their miles are measured along the ground track or the flight path, or from which speed, so
the residual is left unresolved here. **The experiment is a few tens of kilometres of flight.** All that the
programme set out to learn had to be measured inside that window, on a vehicle that would not be
recovered.

### The Stack

The research vehicle was carried to its test condition on a modified Pegasus first stage, an Orion 50S
motor with a Taurus propellant grain, connected through an adapter that also conditioned the vehicle
during captive flight and initiated separation. The whole assembly was 589 inches long and weighed
41,750 pounds at drop, and it was carried by the NASA Dryden B-52B, tail number
52-008\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].

**The proportions explain the first flight.**

$$\frac{m_{\text{HXRV}}}{m_{\text{stack}}} = \frac{3{,}000}{41{,}750} = 0.072 \qquad \frac{L_{\text{HXRV}}}{L_{\text{stack}}} = \frac{12}{49.1} = 0.244$$

| | Value | Share of stack |
|---|---|---|
| Stack mass at drop | 41,750 lbm | |
| Research vehicle mass | 3,000 lbm | 7.2 % |
| Stack length | 49.1 ft | |
| Research vehicle length | 12 ft | 24 % |

**The experiment is seven percent of the mass of the thing that carries it.** The booster is the larger
part of the vehicle by every measure, it flies first, and it had never flown this
trajectory\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].

**That last point is the origin of the failure.** The trajectory chosen for the mission was at a
lower altitude than a typical Pegasus trajectory, and so at a higher dynamic pressure, and it was
chosen that way because of weight limits on the B-52\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].
**The weight limit worked through the booster's surplus energy.** An unmodified Pegasus first stage
would have carried the stack well past Mach 7, and the booster selection had assumed that ballast would
absorb the surplus. The Mach 7 flight needed 10,600 pounds of it, which would have taken the stack past
the B-52B's 41,400 pound limit on its X-15 pylon, a limit later raised, and the stack above weighed
41,750 pounds at drop, over the original limit by

$$41{,}750 - 41{,}400 = 350 \ \text{lb}$$

The alternatives were to remove propellant from the
motor or to launch lower and slower, at about 20,000 feet and Mach 0.5 instead of the standard 40,000
feet and Mach 0.8, and the first flight took the second\[[Peebles 2007][research_peebles_2007]\]. The
return-to-flight review states the consequence, which is that the booster saw dynamic pressures at
transonic conditions about twice those of a standard Pegasus
flight\[[Reubush et al. 2003][research_reubush_2003]\].

**The factor follows from the atmosphere.** At a given Mach number dynamic pressure is proportional to
static pressure,

$$q = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho V^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \gamma p M^{2} \qquad \frac{q_{20{,}000}}{q_{40{,}000}} = \frac{p_{20{,}000}}{p_{40{,}000}} = \frac{46{,}601}{18{,}823} = 2.48$$

with the static pressures those of the 1976 standard
atmosphere\[[U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 1976][research_us_atmos_1976]\] in pascals. The comparison assumes
that each stack passes a given Mach number about 20,000 feet apart in altitude, which the launch
altitudes suggest and the published trajectories do not state, so it shows the order of the effect
and does not fix its value. **A carrier aircraft constraint pushed the booster into a flight regime its
inherited control models had not been built for**, and the board places the loss of control in
transonic flight\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].

**Separation itself was a research problem.** Two non-axisymmetric bodies separating at high dynamic
pressure at hypersonic speed had not been done, and the programme studied it at
length\[[Tartabini et al. 2003][research_tartabini_2003]\]. **The range operations were a separate
undertaking**, since an expendable hypersonic vehicle over the Pacific must be tracked and terminated
by a range that was not built for
it\[[Lux-Baumann and Burkes 2005][research_lux_2005]\].

## The Flight Test Record

### Flight 1, 2 June 2001

**The mission failed thirteen and a half seconds after release and the board's account is precise
enough to reconstruct as intervals.**

The stack was released from the B-52 one hour and fifteen minutes after takeoff. The launch vehicle
motor ignited 5.19 seconds later and the mission proceeded as planned through the start of the pitch-up
manoeuvre at 8 seconds. At approximately 11.5 seconds a control anomaly began, characterised by a
diverging roll oscillation at 2.5 hertz. The oscillation continued to diverge until approximately 13
seconds, when the rudder electromechanical actuator stalled and ceased to respond to autopilot
commands. **The rudder stall caused loss of yaw control and the sideslip diverged rapidly to over 8
degrees.** At 13.5 seconds the starboard elevon was structurally overloaded. The vehicle deviated
significantly from its planned trajectory and was terminated by range control 48.57 seconds after
release\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].

| Interval | Duration |
|---|---|
| Release to motor ignition | 5.19 s |
| Ignition to pitch-up | 2.81 s |
| Pitch-up to first anomaly | 3.50 s |
| Anomaly to actuator stall | 1.50 s |
| Stall to structural overload | 0.50 s |
| **Anomaly to structural overload** | **2.00 s** |

Each interval is the difference of successive event times, and the number of oscillation cycles in
an interval is its duration times the frequency $f$,

$$\Delta t = t_{\text{overload}} - t_{\text{anomaly}} = 13.5 - 11.5 = 2.00 \ \text{s} \qquad n = f \, \Delta t = 2.5 \times 2.00 = 5$$

**At 2.5 hertz, two seconds is five cycles.** The vehicle went from nominal to structural failure in
five cycles of a diverging oscillation, a useful fact about the class of failure.
The return-to-flight review adds the breakup that followed. The right fin broke off at about 13
seconds, followed within one second by the left fin and the rudder, the wing broke off at 15 seconds,
the booster's data stream was lost at 21, and the research vehicle's telemetry ended at 77.5
seconds\[[Reubush et al. 2003][research_reubush_2003]\].

**How unstable was it? Less than one might expect.** A diverging oscillation grows as

$$\theta(t) = \theta_{0} \, e^{\sigma t} \cos \omega t \qquad \sigma = \frac{1}{t} \ln \frac{\theta(t)}{\theta_{0}}$$

and the corresponding damping ratio, negative for a divergence, is

$$\zeta = \frac{-\sigma}{\sqrt{\sigma^{2} + \omega^{2}}} \qquad \omega = 2 \pi f$$

| Amplitude growth over 2.0 s | $\sigma$, s⁻¹ | $\zeta$ |
|---|---|---|
| 5 times | 0.805 | −0.051 |
| 10 times | 1.151 | −0.073 |
| 20 times | 1.498 | −0.095 |

**A damping ratio of a few hundredths on the wrong side of zero is the entire difference between this
failure and a successful flight.** The vehicle was not wildly unstable. It was slightly unstable, for
two seconds, which was enough.
**There was no interval in which anything could have been done**, and the vehicle carried no capability
to do it\[[Peebles 2007][research_peebles_2007]\].

### The Margin That Was Not There

**The board's root cause lies in the models and names no failed hardware.** It found that the
launch vehicle failed because the vehicle control system design was deficient for the trajectory flown,
due to inaccurate analytical models of both Pegasus heritage and launch-vehicle-specific origin, which
overestimated the system margins\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].

**The arithmetic of that overestimate is the most instructive number in this article.** The roll axis
gain margin, the aileron margin in the board's words, had been predicted before flight at 8 decibels against a requirement of 6. Correcting the
models brought the prediction to under 2 decibels\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].

A gain margin in decibels is the factor by which the loop gain may rise before the system reaches the
stability boundary,

$$\mathrm{GM}_{\text{dB}} = 20 \log_{10} k_{\max}$$

so those three figures correspond to gain factors of

| | Margin, dB | Permissible gain factor |
|---|---|---|
| Preflight prediction | 8 | 2.51 |
| Requirement | 6 | 2.00 |
| After model correction | under 2 | 1.26 |

**The available overshoot above unity fell from 1.51 to 0.26, a loss of 83 percent of the entire margin**,

$$\frac{k_{8} - k_{2}}{k_{8} - 1} = \frac{2.512 - 1.259}{2.512 - 1} = 0.83$$

with $k_{8}$ and $k_{2}$ the permissible gain factors at 8 and 2 decibels, and it took the vehicle from
two decibels above its requirement to more than four decibels below it.

**And the corrected model was still stable.** The board states that the reduction, although very
significant and close to the instability boundary, still predicted a stable vehicle, so nominal model
corrections alone were insufficient to predict the loss of control, and **parameter uncertainty had to
be included before the mishap reproduced**\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].

**The board's conclusion is the sentence this article is built around.** No single contributing factor
or potential contributing factor caused the mishap. The flight mishap could only be reproduced when all
of the modelling inaccuracies with uncertainty variations were incorporated in the system level linear
analysis model and the nonlinear
simulation\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].

**A margin failure looks like this when it is honestly investigated.** The root cause was found in
the models and was not a failed part. Every contributing error was individually
survivable\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].

**The arithmetic shows why no single analysis could have found it.** Let the true
margin be the nominal margin reduced by the modelling errors,

$$m_{\text{true}} = m_{\text{nominal}} - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert e_{i} \rvert$$

and let each error consume a fraction $f$ of the nominal margin, so that $\lvert e_{i} \rvert = f \, m_{\text{nominal}}$.
**Any single analysis reports a healthy margin whenever $f < 1$.** The system is nonetheless unstable
when the errors combine,

$$m_{\text{true}} < 0 \iff n f > 1$$

| Terms $n$ | Each consumes $f$ | Each analysis reports | Combination consumes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 40 % | a 60 % margin remaining | 120 % |
| 4 | 30 % | a 70 % margin remaining | 120 % |
| 5 | 25 % | a 75 % margin remaining | 125 % |

**Every row of that table is a vehicle that every individual analysis passes and that is
unstable.** The condition for the failure to be invisible is $f < 1$ and the condition for it to
happen is $n f > 1$, and both hold simultaneously whenever $n > 1$ and $f$ is between $1/n$ and 1.

**The board's finding says the same thing**, that no single contributing factor caused
the mishap and that it reproduced only when all of the modelling inaccuracies with uncertainty
variations were incorporated together. **The margin was positive throughout and the uncertainty on the
margin was larger than the margin.**

The contributors were modelling inaccuracies in the fin actuation system, including under-prediction of
its compliance, modelling inaccuracies in the aerodynamics, including an error incorporating wind
tunnel data into the mathematical model, a misinterpretation of wind tunnel results due to insufficient data, and unmodelled outer mould line changes associated with the
thermal protection system, and insufficient variation of modelling parameters in the aerodynamics, the
fin actuation system and the control system\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].

**One of those deserves separate notice.** The thermal protection system changed the outer mould line
and the change was not modelled\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\]. **The thermal solution altered the aerodynamics and the aerodynamic
model did not know.** The fault was one of coupling between two disciplines, with no error inside
either.

### Return to Flight

**The board's draft report went in on 8 March 2002 and the return-to-flight work began that month**,
taking the report and the corrective actions drawn from it as its starting
point\[[Reubush et al. 2003][research_reubush_2003]\]. The record of what was changed answers the
board's finding item by item.

- **The models.** Higher fidelity models of the booster aerodynamics, fin actuators, structure and
  autopilot were built, and extensive Monte Carlo simulations were run with newly developed uncertainty
  models of all appropriate parameters, written to be conservative. The boost was simulated
  independently by NASA as a check on the contractor's analysis, and the two agreed.
- **The actuators.** New fin actuators were built with higher torque, by adding a second motor in a
  torque-summing arrangement, new gears, a stainless steel housing in place of aluminium, two more
  batteries and redesigned electronics.
- **The trajectory.** About 3,350 pounds of propellant was removed from the booster, which let the
  second flight launch at the standard 40,000 feet and see significantly lower dynamic pressure and
  loading than the first.
- **The separation.** The final separation analysis, with conservative uncertainty models, found 97
  percent of cases successful and fewer than one percent recontacting the adapter.

All four are from the return-to-flight review\[[Reubush et al. 2003][research_reubush_2003]\].
**The first of them is the board's lesson put into practice**, since the mishap did not reproduce
until parameter uncertainty was added. The investigation took nine months and the
return-to-flight effort two years\[[Grindle and Bahm 2006][research_grindle_bahm_2006]\].

### Flight 2, 27 March 2004

**The vehicle separated at approximately Mach 7 and accelerated under scramjet
power**\[[Bahm et al. 2005][research_bahm_2005]\]\[[Karlgaard et al. 2004][research_karlgaard_tartabini_2004]\].
The B-52 dropped the stack at Mach 0.8 and 40,000 feet, the booster ignited after five seconds of free
fall, pulled up at 1.9 g and pushed over at 0.7 g into nearly level flight at 95,000
feet\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\]. **The booster delivered the stack slightly
short of its Mach number and dynamic pressure targets**, which the chief engineer's account tabulates against the best estimate
atmosphere\[[Marshall et al. 2005a][research_marshall_corpening_2005]\],

| Separation | Target | Flight 2 | Deviation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Altitude, ft | 93,932 | 94,069 | +137 |
| Mach number | 7.075 | 6.946 | −0.129 |
| Dynamic pressure, lbf/ft² | 1,066 | 1,024 | −42 |
| Flight path angle, deg | 2.0 | 2.4 | +0.4 |

each deviation being the achieved value less the target, so that the relative shortfalls in Mach
number and dynamic pressure are

$$\frac{6.946 - 7.075}{7.075} = -1.8 \ \% \qquad \frac{1{,}024 - 1{,}066}{1{,}066} = -3.9 \ \%$$

**The engine test ran on schedule.** The cowl door opened 2.5 seconds after separation, five seconds of
fuel-off tare data followed, and the scramjet was fuelled for approximately 11 seconds, reaching a
maximum powered Mach number of 6.83, before a further fuel-off tare and a cowl-open parameter
identification manoeuvre, 4 seconds and 17 seconds long. The cowl closed 39 seconds after
separation, which the reported phases account for to within half a second,

$$2.5 + 5 + 11 + 4 + 17 = 39.5 \ \text{s}$$

after which the vehicle flew a controlled descent with further manoeuvres and splashed down in the open ocean without
recovery\[[Marshall et al. 2005a][research_marshall_corpening_2005]\]. **The guidance and control overview gives the fuelled portion as approximately 10 seconds**\[[Bahm et al. 2005][research_bahm_2005]\], one second fewer. With that figure the phases fall half a second short of the 39-second cowl closure, where 11 seconds leave them half a second over, and this article keeps the chief engineer's 11 seconds, which the technology summary also gives. The NASA history adds that the
vehicle kept accelerating for most of the burn and began to slow only in its final
moments\[[Peebles 2007][research_peebles_2007]\].

**The paper that closes the loop between design and flight is the engine's account**, which traces
the Mach 7 flowpath from design through ground test to
flight\[[Ferlemann et al. 2005][research_ferlemann_2005]\]. The flowpath pressures show the Mach 7
engine operating in dual mode, with sonic flow in the isolator dissipating the inlet
shocks\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\].

**That is the answer to the question the programme was built to ask.** Thrust exceeded drag on an
airframe-integrated scramjet in free flight, for the first time, at a dynamic pressure of about 980
pounds per square foot, and the vehicle gained speed while the engine
ran\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\].

**The stage separation also worked**, and the programme describes it as the first known successful
non-symmetric, high dynamic pressure, high Mach number stage
separation\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\].

### Flight 3, 16 November 2004

**The third flight was a cruise test by design.** The first plan had included two Mach 10 flights, one
to cruise and one to accelerate\[[Freeman et al. 1997][research_freeman_1997]\], and only the cruise
flight survived the restructuring. Its test goal was a scramjet producing as much thrust as the
vehicle's drag, and so holding a cruise condition\[[Peebles 2007][research_peebles_2007]\]. **The
booster could not quite reach Mach 10.** Weight growth in the stack and higher booster drag led the
managers to accept a nominal separation at Mach 9.6\[[Peebles 2007][research_peebles_2007]\], with a
dynamic pressure requirement of 1,000 pounds per square foot. The launch followed the same B-52
conditions with a steeper 2.5 g pull-up to a flight path angle of over 30 degrees and a 0.5 g pushover
into nearly level flight at 110,000 feet\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\].

| Separation | Target | Flight 3 | Deviation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Altitude, ft | 109,580 | 109,440 | −140 |
| Mach number | 9.6 | 9.736 | +0.136 |
| Dynamic pressure, lbf/ft² | 1,000 | 959 | −41 |
| Flight path angle, deg | 1.5 | 1.69 | +0.19 |

The values are those of the Mach 10 overview, computed with its best estimate
atmosphere\[[Marshall et al. 2005b][research_marshall_2005]\].

**The vehicle cruised as predicted.** The cowl opened 2.5 seconds after separation, fuelling began about
5 seconds after separation, and the scramjet was fuelled for approximately 10 seconds and produced the
predicted thrust. **During that time the X-43A sustained thrust equal to drag**, reaching a maximum
powered Mach number of 9.68, and the cowl closed 22 seconds after
separation\[[Marshall et al. 2005b][research_marshall_2005]\]. With the 3 second pre-test tare and 6
second post-test tare of the technology summary\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\],
the phases again account for the reported time,

$$2.5 + 3 + 10 + 6 = 21.5 \ \text{s}$$

against 22 seconds, with no cowl-open manoeuvres on this flight because of concern for the
cowl\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\]. The ignition sequence ran on silane for
the first two fuelled conditions, 5 seconds in all, before repeating them on hydrogen alone, and the
flowpath pressures show classical pure supersonic combustion, with a shock-dominated
combustor\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\]. The highest recorded temperatures were on
the nose, as predicted\[[Marshall et al. 2005b][research_marshall_2005]\].

**The two flights answer different questions, and the difference between them is physics as well as
test design.** At Mach 7 the engine accelerated the vehicle. At Mach 10 it was asked to sustain the
vehicle and did\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\]. The thrust relation shows why the second is the harder demand. Rewriting it as a
fractional velocity increment,

$$F_{\text{thrust}} \approx \dot{m}_{0} V_{0} \left( \frac{V_{e}}{V_{0}} - 1 \right)$$

**the heat release per unit mass of air is fixed by the fuel and the air, so the energy the engine can
add does not grow with flight speed while the kinetic energy of the captured flow grows as its
square.** The fractional increment therefore falls as Mach number rises. Drag meanwhile scales with
dynamic pressure, which this trajectory holds near constant. **One term shrinks and the other does
not.** Because the Mach 10 acceleration flight was never flown, how much margin remained above cruise
at Mach 9.68 is unknown, and the flights show only that the engine met the cruise requirement it was
designed for\[[Peebles 2007][research_peebles_2007]\].

**Reported as a speed record, the two flights were the fastest air-breathing flights made to that
time, in the words of NASA's history.** That history sets the second flight's Mach 6.83 against the Mach 3.32 an SR-71 reached in 1976, and the
third flight's Mach 9.68 against the second's\[[Peebles 2007][research_peebles_2007]\], increments of

$$6.83 - 3.32 = 3.51 \qquad 9.68 - 6.83 = 2.85$$

in Mach number. Reported as physics, the pair shows that the thrust-drag margin is positive at Mach 7
and can be held at zero at Mach 9.68.

## Comparison With Ground Prediction

**Every flight of this programme was a test of a prediction made on the ground, and the three flights
returned three different verdicts.** The opening of this article explains why the
comparison was the purpose of the vehicle rather than a by-product of it. Ground facilities and
computation could each supply a large term with an uncertainty band, and only flight could say whether
the small difference between those terms had the sign the design assumed. This section sets the ground
predictions the article reports beside what each flight returned, and points to where each comparison
is argued.

**The ground prediction for the engine came from a large campaign in several independent facilities.** Langley built an aerodynamic database across its tunnel complex covering separation, the
powered condition and the descent\[[McClinton et al. 1998a][research_mcclinton_1998]\]\[[Holland et al. 2000][research_holland_2000]\],
the engine flowpath was run in the 8-foot High Temperature Tunnel and in shock
tunnels\[[Huebner et al. 2000][research_huebner_2000]\]\[[Bakos et al. 2001][research_bakos_2001]\], and the
flight engine was ground tested before each
mission\[[Huebner et al. 2001][research_huebner_2001]\]. That campaign is described under Dependent
Systems.

**On the engine, flight agreed with the ground.** The programme's retrospectives report that engine
thrust was close to its design value on both powered flights\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\],
and the Mach 7 scramjet design paper traces the flowpath from design through ground test to
flight\[[Ferlemann et al. 2005][research_ferlemann_2005]\]. At Mach 7 the vehicle accelerated under
power, and at Mach 9.68 it held approximately constant velocity\[[Marshall et al. 2005b][research_marshall_2005]\].
**That agreement is the calibration the programme sought**, and its consequences are the subject
of What the Data Changed.

**The programme's comparisons are quantitative, and they divide the force into its two large terms.**
On thrust, the increment in acceleration under power at Mach 7 was about as predicted, which confirms
the predicted engine thrust to within less than two percent, and at Mach 10 the vehicle cruised at the
reference fuel setting with thrust in agreement with
prediction\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\]. A Dryden summary puts the Mach 7 engine
performance within three percent of the preflight
predictions\[[Grindle and Bahm 2006][research_grindle_bahm_2006]\]. On drag, the vehicle decelerated
more than predicted with the cowl both closed and open. About two thirds of that error came from the
actual flight conditions differing from those predicted and about one third from drag higher than
predicted, which still lay within the uncertainty of the wind tunnel
database\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\]. **The descent data say the same thing
more strongly.** Parameter identification over the cowl-closed descent of the second flight, from Mach
6.80 down to 0.95, found the axial force 10 to 15 percent higher than predicted from wind tunnel data
and the normal force underpredicted by a similar amount, and above Mach 4 the static margin came out
larger than predicted\[[Marl and White 2006][research_davis_white_2006]\].

**So the engine was predicted better than the airframe it was integrated into.** The keystone's small
difference appears here from the flight side. The thrust term was within two or three percent\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\]\[[Grindle and Bahm 2006][research_grindle_bahm_2006]\], and the
drag term carried the larger error, which the uncertainty of the wind tunnel database absorbed\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\]. This article does not
reconstruct the measured net thrust, so it reports these comparisons as the programme states
them and sets no predicted value from this article beside a measured one. Where the Framing Breaks Down
argues that limitation, and the Epistemic State records it.

**On the launch vehicle, flight disagreed with the ground, and the disagreement destroyed the first
mission.** The roll axis gain margin was predicted before flight at 8 decibels against a requirement
of 6. Flight returned a diverging roll oscillation at 2.5 hertz that reached structural overload of the
starboard elevon two seconds after it began\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].
**The ground models had overestimated the margin**, and correcting them brought the prediction to under
2 decibels while still predicting a stable vehicle. The loss reproduced only when every modelling
inaccuracy was combined with its uncertainty. Among the inaccuracies were an error incorporating wind
tunnel data into the mathematical model and unmodelled outer mould line changes associated with the
thermal protection system. The arithmetic of that margin is worked in full in the flight test record
above.

**Stage separation was predicted by analysis and confirmed by flight.** The programme studied the
separation of two non-axisymmetric bodies at high dynamic pressure at
length\[[Tartabini et al. 2003][research_tartabini_2003]\], and on the second flight the separation
worked.

**The thermal predictions held.** At Mach 7 the thermal analysis of the nose, horizontal tails and
vertical tails gave reasonable predictions of the recorded flight temperatures, most of them
conservative, with an unexplained excess near the forward edge of the vertical tail
skins\[[Amundsen et al. 2004][research_amundsen_2004]\]. At Mach 10 the finite element model of
the carbon-carbon nose bracketed the measured temperature through the boost and the powered
flight\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\].

**Two of this article's own ground figures are consistency checks rather than comparisons with
flight.** The leading edge heating rates derived earlier are correlation
estimates from the Sutton and Graves relation, and the flight reports give temperatures inside the
carbon-carbon and no surface heat fluxes to set beside them. The dynamic pressures of the sizing
argument are computed from the standard atmosphere and were set there beside the reported values,
from which they differ by 2.6 and 4.6 percent.

## What the Data Changed

**The tools were calibrated, which was the stated objective, and the result is real even though it is dull.**
Engine thrust came close to its design value on both powered
flights\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\], the statement on which the calibration depends. **A prediction that is confirmed in flight converts a design method from a hypothesis
into an instrument.** The programme released the data to more than twenty government and industrial
organisations in complete classified data packages, alongside more than fifty classified and
unclassified papers and presentations\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\], so the
calibration is held by the community that designs such vehicles as well as by NASA.

**As hardware, the X-43A led nowhere directly.** The X-43C, which would have flown a hydrocarbon-fuelled
engine at larger scale, was planned in
detail\[[Moses 2003b][research_moses_2003]\]\[[Cockrell et al. 2002][research_cockrell_2002]\].
The project's 2011 retrospective still lists it as a planned demonstrator, beside a planned
reusable X-43B and a conceptual X-43D, and records that the X-43A project ended in December 2004 when
its money ran out\[[Grindle 2011][research_grindle_2011]\]. None of the three had flown when that
retrospective was written. **The line of descent runs through the X-51A
instead**\[[Hank et al. 2008][research_hank_2008]\], which on its fourth flight in May 2013 flew for
three and a half minutes on scramjet power, reaching Mach 5.1 on hydrocarbon
fuel\[[Boeing X-51A WaveRider Sets 2013][ref_boeing_x51a_2013]\]. Its burn was measured in minutes where the X-43A's was
measured in seconds, and it is treated later in this series.

**The failure changed practice more visibly than the success did.** A mishap whose cause is
distributed across several models, none individually wrong enough to matter, is an argument for
uncertainty analysis rather than for better point predictions. The board's recommendations are in the
export-controlled part of its report, but the return-to-flight programme shows what was done, which
was to run extensive Monte Carlo simulations with newly developed uncertainty models of all
appropriate parameters\[[Reubush et al. 2003][research_reubush_2003]\].
**The durable lesson is to carry parameter uncertainty through system-level stability analysis instead of validating nominal models.**

**The programme also demonstrated something about heritage.** The launch vehicle was modified from a
Pegasus first stage\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\], a booster that had already made a number of successful satellite launches\[[Peebles 2007][research_peebles_2007]\], and the heritage models were part of what failed. The board attributes the root cause to inaccurate analytical models of both Pegasus heritage and launch-vehicle-specific kinds and finds that the booster flew in an environment significantly different from previous Pegasus experience\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\], so the heritage models were valid for the trajectories that record covered and this trajectory was not one of them. **Inherited
confidence is confidence in a domain, and the domain travels with the model whether or not anyone
writes it down.**

**The survey below maps the field this vehicle sits in.** It holds the 43 research records among the curated sources together with the wider literature, and every record is assigned to exactly one cluster. **The Source Base states the admission rule, the classes it excludes and how much of the survey has been read.**

**One statement covers every cluster below and is not repeated under each.** A cluster's size measures how much has been published near a topic, not how important the topic is to this vehicle, and the two diverge sharply. The cluster holding this article's keystone is the largest of twenty-four, while flight control, guidance and stability, the discipline that lost the first flight, ranks twelfth. **Control is not a small literature, however.** Together with the 410 records on the control and dynamics of air-breathing hypersonic vehicles it holds 764 records, more than any single cluster except the scramjet cycle, supersonic combustion, boundary layer and inlet clusters.

### What the Shape of the Survey Says

**A cluster's size measures how much exists. Its date profile shows whether the subject is alive.** On this corpus the two disagree sharply, and the disagreement is about this vehicle.

**The youngest literatures in the table are guidance and control.** Glide vehicles, trajectories and their tracking has 76 percent of its records from 2015 onward, the control and dynamics of air-breathing hypersonic vehicles 69 percent with only 4 percent before 2000, and flight control, guidance and stability 59 percent with 12 percent before 2000, the three highest recent shares among the named clusters. **Control is the discipline that destroyed this vehicle's first flight.** The mishap board's finding was about control margins and modelling uncertainty, and control has grown faster since than propulsion. Whether that growth is a consequence of failures like this one is not established here, but the ordering is at least consistent with it.

**The two clusters with the least recent work are the ones about why and about flying.** Programmes, missions and access to space carries the lowest post-2015 share in the table at 21 percent, and launch, separation and flight test operations the next lowest at 26 percent. **The field kept working on the engine and stopped working on the aeroplane.**

**The preceding article in this series found the same pattern**, where the upper stage cluster was the smallest of its central clusters and among the oldest while the propulsion clusters were among the largest and youngest. **Two consecutive articles, on unrelated vehicles, reached it from opposite directions.** A survey that shows a live propulsion literature attached to a dead mission literature is describing a field that has become an end in itself, and this article does not have the evidence to say whether the condition is a failure or a normal phase.

**Its titles are mostly about the engine's interior rather than the force it delivers.** Of its 2,090 titles, 889 name a combustor or combustion and 256 name dual-mode operation or mode transition, while 76 name thrust and 18 name drag. **The quantity the keystone asks about is a minority subject even here**, and the whole survey holds three titles that name force accounting, net thrust or thrust minus drag, as Thin Subjects records.

### Supersonic combustion, injection and mixing

**The second largest cluster, and the one where the physics is genuinely hard rather than merely difficult to measure.** Fuel injection, mixing, ignition, flameholding and the chemistry of hydrogen and hydrocarbon fuels in high-speed flow.

Fuel must mix with air and burn in a flow crossing the combustor in about a millisecond, so mixing rate rather than reaction rate governs, and every injection scheme is a compromise between penetration and total pressure loss. **514 of its titles name mixing and 344 name ignition, flameholding or flame stabilisation.** It also holds 234 records of doubtful relevance, most of them combustor studies outside high-speed flight whose subject is flameholding, ignition, mixing or combustion instability in its own right.

**The cluster is the fourth largest in the table, and its titles are dominated by starting and the shock train.** 215 name starting, unstart or restart and 89 name a shock train or pseudo-shock. **The margin framing recurs here only implicitly.** Unstart margin is the distance between the pressure the combustor produces and the pressure the inlet will tolerate, yet two titles name a margin.

### Aerothermodynamics, heating and thermal protection

**The cluster that decides what the vehicle can be made of.** Aerodynamic heating, stagnation and leading-edge heating, thermal protection, high-temperature materials and hot structures.

On an airframe-integrated engine the nozzle is the aft underside of the aeroplane and expands against the external flow on one side only, so its performance depends on flight condition and attitude in a way a bell nozzle's does not. **The exhaust also contributes a pitching moment**, which couples propulsion to trim and is why this literature and the flight control literature cannot be read separately.

### Ground test facilities and measurement

**Its subject is the reason the programme existed.** Wind tunnels, shock tunnels and high-enthalpy facilities, and the measurement techniques used in them.

### Margins, uncertainty and model validation

**This cluster exists because the article's conclusion is about margins.** The article's most transferable finding is that a stability margin with an uncertainty larger than itself is indistinguishable from a negative one, and that no single-factor analysis can see it. The survey's vocabulary is written around a vehicle rather than around a numerical method, so computational work enters where it is applied to hypersonic flight. **178 of its 291 titles name hypersonic flow or a hypersonic vehicle and 17 name a scramjet, a ramjet, combustion or propulsion**, so the cluster should be read as computation applied to this kind of vehicle, not as a survey of hypersonic computational fluid dynamics.

### Vehicle configuration and airframe integration

**The cluster where the keystone is a design principle rather than a measurement.** Waverider derivations, configuration design, aerodynamic databases and airframe integration.

The vision that justified scramjet development was air-breathing access to space, and this cluster has the lowest share of recent work in the table, 21 percent from 2015 onward. Three of its titles concern control or tracking rather than missions, so the mission literature proper is smaller still. **The propulsion literature is thriving and the mission literature has not kept pace**, which is the same pattern the preceding article found in upper stages, arrived at from a completely different direction.

### Hydrogen flames

**Measurements and models of hydrogen-air flames**, supersonic and subsonic, whose subject is the flame itself rather than an engine.

71 percent of these records date from before 2000, the highest share in the table.
