## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**Treating this vehicle through thrust-drag closure is right and it hides three things.**

**First, the keystone frames a binary question and the data answer a quantitative one.** Knowing that
net thrust was positive at Mach 7 is a different and much weaker statement than knowing its value to
within some percentage. The calibration value of the data comes from the detailed pressure and force
reconstruction, which put the thrust within two percent of prediction and the drag above it, as the
comparison with ground prediction above reports. The keystone describes neither the
reconstruction nor its uncertainty.

**Second, the keystone says nothing about the ten seconds.** A scramjet that produces net thrust for
eleven seconds on hydrogen has not demonstrated a propulsion system, because the thermal problem in a
real vehicle is a steady-state problem and this vehicle never approached steady state.
**The engine was largely a heat sink, absorbing heat throughout rather than rejecting it.**\[[Moses 2003b][research_moses_2003]\]

**Third, the framing makes the first flight look like a distraction, and it was not.** An article
organised around scramjet performance naturally treats a booster control failure as an interruption.
**The board's finding about margin and uncertainty is a more transferable result than the engine data**
and it applies to any vehicle whose stability is computed rather than measured, which is all of them.

**The designation itself is unremarkable for once.** Every source used in this article calls the
vehicle X-43A without qualification, and no source consulted raises a question about
the pairing. After three consecutive articles on contested designations, the fact deserves one
sentence and no more. **The absence of a dispute is not the same as positive evidence that
none exists**, and this article did not locate a nomenclature reference for the X-43 to check against,
which is recorded in the Epistemic State.

**A fourth concerns scale and comes with an equation attached.** The article treats a twelve
foot vehicle as evidence about hypersonic air-breathing propulsion generally, and the quantity that
refuses to scale is the Reynolds number,

$$\mathrm{Re} = \frac{\rho V L}{\mu} \qquad \mu = \frac{1.458 \times 10^{-6} \, T^{3/2}}{T + 110.4}$$

At the two flight conditions the dynamic viscosity is $1.47 \times 10^{-5}$ and
$1.51 \times 10^{-5}$ pascal seconds, giving a length Reynolds number of
$1.11 \times 10^{7}$ at 95,000 feet and $7.65 \times 10^{6}$ at 110,000.

**Reynolds number is proportional to length at a fixed flight condition**, so a vehicle five times
longer sits at $5.5 \times 10^{7}$ and one ten times longer at $1.11 \times 10^{8}$, an order of
magnitude above the flight article. **Boundary layer transition location does not scale with it**, and
transition sets skin friction, heating and the state of the flow entering the inlet.
**Transition prediction at flight conditions still relies on engineering correlations, for want of a theory**\[[Campbell et al. 2010][research_campbell_2010]\], and the aerothermal difficulties of
hypersonic flight were catalogued before this vehicle was
conceived\[[Holden 1986b][research_holden_1986]\]. **The flight data
calibrate the tools at one Reynolds number and the tools are then used at another**, which is a
weakness that a flight article of one size cannot remove.

**A fifth caution concerns what "first" means here.** A joint Russian and American programme flew a
scramjet on a Mach 6.5 flight test in the 1990s\[[Roudakov et al. 1998][research_roudakov_semenov_1998]\],
and various rocket-boosted scramjet experiments preceded this one. **The X-43A claim is narrower than
the popular one**, being the first free-flight demonstration of an airframe-integrated scramjet
producing thrust in excess of vehicle drag\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\], and each qualifier in that sentence is doing work.

## The Source Base

**46 curated sources carry the argument, and 43 of them are research records that the survey also holds.**

**All 46 are primary or canonical technical sources**, being NASA technical papers, conference
papers and presentations, one mishap investigation board report, one NASA history, one manufacturer's
announcement and two textbooks. **35 of them come from the NASA Technical Reports Server**, which is
the defining fact about this article's evidence.

**The difficulty here is abundance rather than scarcity.** The two preceding articles argued from thin
records and had to derive what was not published. Hyper-X published nearly everything, so the risk is
the opposite one, which is assembling a plausible curated set without reading the documents that carry
the argument.

**Seven sources do most of the work and they should be named.** The mishap investigation board report
is the single best source on this vehicle, and it supplies not only the failure but the configuration,
the stack mass and length, the trajectory rationale and the programme objectives, because the board had
to establish all of those before it could analyse the loss. The chief engineer's account of the second
flight and the Mach 10 overview carry the flight sequences and the separation conditions, the
programme's technology summary carries the engine-test conditions and the thrust and drag
comparisons, and the Mach 7 scramjet design paper traces the flowpath from design through ground test
to flight, which is the loop the programme existed to close. The return-to-flight review records what
was changed after the loss, and NASA's history of the programme supplies the
trajectory choice behind the first flight and the decisions that set the third flight's Mach number.

**One document supplies most of the standard relations.** NACA Report 1135 tabulates the isentropic
relations, the oblique shock relations and the Rayleigh flow relation in the forms this article uses,
and it has not been superseded as the reference statement of them. **A 1953 report is the right
citation for a 2004 flight** because the relations have not changed and the report states them more
carefully than any textbook.

**Three more supply the specific correlations.** The Kantrowitz inlet starting criterion comes from a
1945 report that has not been improved on as a first estimate. The stagnation heating correlation is
Sutton and Graves, which generalises the dissociated-air analysis of Fay and Riddell. The atmosphere is
the 1976 standard, which every flight-condition figure in this article depends on.

**The research survey holds 10,968 research records**, 10,932 of them identified by a Crossref digital object identifier, 35 on the NASA Technical Reports Server and one on NASA's own site, of which 655 are report primaries, being 6.0 percent, by the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary. **The median publication year is 2013.** Of the 10,968 dated records, 3,238 were published before 2000, being 29.5 percent, and 5,052 in 2015 or later, being 46.1 percent.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on the NASA Technical Reports Server or it carries a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, which Crossref registers for Defense Technical Information Center reports. **The rule reaches the programme's own papers on the report server**, which is where 35 of the curated sources come from. **It does not reach the conference papers of the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, abbreviated AIAA**, which are seventeen of the 45 survey titles that name the X-43 or Hyper-X, nor the mishap board's report, published on NASA's own site. **6.0 percent is therefore a lower bound on how much of this survey is first-hand.**

### Thin Subjects

**Five subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen read as a space. Where a row joins two groups of terms with the word together, a title must carry a term from each group.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| net thrust and the thrust-drag bookkeeping of an integrated vehicle | force accounting, thrust minus drag, net thrust, thrust drag accounting, thrust and drag accounting, thrust drag bookkeeping, net axial force | 3 |
| a trajectory flown at constant dynamic pressure | constant dynamic pressure, constant q, dynamic pressure together with trajectory, ascent, corridor, flight path, climb | 1 |
| air dissociation at the combustor entrance | dissociation, dissociated, dissociating together with combustor, combustion, scramjet, ramjet, inlet, intake | 0 |
| the stability margin of a booster or launch vehicle autopilot | stability margin, gain margin, phase margin, stability margins together with launch vehicle, booster, rocket, missile, launcher | 4 |
| air launch and captive carry | air launch, air launched, airlaunch, captive carry, captive flight | 8 |

**The quantity the keystone asks about has almost no literature of its own.** Three titles name force accounting, net thrust or thrust minus drag, among them a paper on hypersonic propulsion system force accounting, so the statement that the net force is a small difference between two large terms rests on the relations derived above rather than on a published body of method.

**The corridor this vehicle flew is a design rule rather than a research subject.** One title names dynamic pressure together with a trajectory, ascent, corridor or climb, and it concerns glide rather than powered flight.

**No title names air dissociation together with a combustor, an inlet or an engine**, so the argument that a subsonic-combustion engine at Mach 10 would deliver dissociated air to its combustor stands on the stagnation temperature relation and the dissociation thresholds cited above.

**The finding that lost the first flight is barely a subject in its own right.** Four titles name a stability, gain or phase margin together with a launch vehicle, booster, rocket, missile or launcher, against 104 titles in the survey that name gain or phase margins at all.

**Air launch is a small literature**, eight titles, one of them on the carriage and launch characteristics of the Pegasus booster this vehicle rode.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject.** The subject is the set of topics the argument uses, namely air-breathing high-speed propulsion and its combustion, inlets and nozzles, aerothermodynamics and thermal protection, boundary layers and shock waves, ground and flight test, the margins and uncertainty of models, the flight control and guidance of high-speed vehicles and their boosters, and the vehicles and programmes themselves. A fundamental study of a phenomenon the argument uses is admitted without an aerospace term when its subject is the phenomenon itself, and a study that applies a method the argument uses to a distant domain is excluded.

**Uncertainty methodology belongs to every field that computes.** The phrases uncertainty quantification, epistemic uncertainty and six degree of freedom also head work on laser powder bed fusion, seismic shear-wave profiles and robotic arms, and records that share only those phrases with this subject are excluded.

**Several of this subject's own names are homonyms.** Waverider is also the make of an oceanographic
wave-measuring buoy and the name of two software tools. Kantrowitz names work in psychoanalysis and
psychiatry, a cardiac surgeon and a cardiac assist pump as well as the inlet starting criterion. Gain
margin and phase margin are also terms of amplifier, power converter and electric machine design.
Specific impulse also measures the electric, nuclear and laser thrusters of spacecraft, six degrees of freedom also describes spacecraft, quadrotors and motion simulators, transition also names a drone's change of flight mode, and hypersonic also names acoustic waves in crystals, liquids and superconductors. Records on those homonyms are excluded.

**The survey excludes records outside its subject and records that are not research works.** Besides the homonyms above, it excludes studies of automotive and marine piston engines, wind engineering and atmospheric flows, road and rail vehicles, ships and ocean mixing, mechanical shock and vibration isolators, ground blasts and the shock compression of solids, coal, boiler, furnace and waste combustion, fuel cells, medicine and biology, industrial robots, the organic chemistry of carbon to carbon bonds, rotorcraft, multirotor drones and low-speed wind tunnel testing, gas turbine combustors studied for their liners, cooling, emissions or power generation, spacecraft attitude control, process control applications of gain and phase margins, and the recovery hardware of solid rocket boosters. It also excludes correction, erratum, clarification and addendum notices, retraction and withdrawal notices, retracted articles, figures, supplementary material, peer-review reports, front matter, trade news items, obituaries and removal notices, and it excludes titles outside the scope their cluster states, such as chapters on shock waves in condensed matter, astrophysics and nuclear matter and a paper on stellar winds. A review of a book, a reference or definition entry, a notice, including a news item whether signed or not, an abstract reprinted by an abstract journal or in another journal's abstract section, and a second deposit of a document the survey already holds are not research works, and none of them is admitted.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept, 819 of them.** Among them are the general theory of specifying a controller by its gain and phase margins, combustor studies outside high-speed flight whose subject is flameholding, ignition, mixing or instability, solid and liquid rocket propulsion for boost, the aero-optics of supersonic mixing layers and the nozzles of chemical lasers, because each shares the subject's physics in its own regime, and a reader may weigh them accordingly.

**The residual cluster admits on-subject records whose single topic belongs to no other cluster**, and it holds 14 records, 0.1 percent of the survey.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

### Historical Fact

NASA initiated the Hyper-X programme in 1996 as a high-risk, high-payoff effort to advance hypersonic
air-breathing propulsion from laboratory experiments to the flight environment, as a collaboration
between Langley Research Center and Dryden Flight Research Center. Micro Craft contracted for the
Hyper-X Research Vehicle and its adapter, and Orbital Sciences Corporation for the Hyper-X Launch
Vehicle. Three flights were planned with a non-recoverable research vehicle on
each\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].

The research vehicle was 12 feet long, 5 feet wide, 2 feet high and weighed about 3,000 pounds, powered
by a single hydrogen-fuelled, dual-mode, airframe-integrated scramjet. The launch vehicle was a
modified Pegasus first stage in the Orion 50S configuration with a Taurus propellant grain. The stack
was 589 inches long and weighed 41,750 pounds at drop, carried by the NASA Dryden B-52B, 52-008. The
trajectory was lower and at higher dynamic pressure than a typical Pegasus trajectory, chosen because
of stack weight limits on the B-52\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\]. The
first flight launched at about 20,000 feet and Mach 0.5, where the standard launch is at 40,000 feet
and Mach 0.8, because the ballast an unmodified motor would have needed exceeded the B-52B's 41,400 pound pylon
limit\[[Peebles 2007][research_peebles_2007]\].

The first flight attempt was on 2 June 2001. Motor ignition occurred 5.19 seconds after release, the
pitch-up manoeuvre began at 8 seconds, a diverging roll oscillation at 2.5 hertz began at approximately
11.5 seconds, the rudder electromechanical actuator stalled at approximately 13 seconds, sideslip
diverged to over 8 degrees, the starboard elevon was structurally overloaded at 13.5 seconds, and the
vehicle was terminated by range control 48.57 seconds after release. The mishap investigation board
convened at Dryden on 5 June 2001\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\]. The
return-to-flight effort removed about 3,350 pounds of propellant so that later flights could launch at
40,000 feet, fitted higher-torque fin actuators, and ran Monte Carlo analyses with new uncertainty
models\[[Reubush et al. 2003][research_reubush_2003]\].

The board's root cause was that the launch vehicle control system design was deficient for the
trajectory flown due to inaccurate analytical models, of both Pegasus heritage and launch-vehicle
specific origin, which overestimated the system margins. The roll axis gain margin was predicted at 8
decibels before flight against a requirement of 6, and model corrections revised it to under 2 decibels
while still predicting a stable vehicle. **No single contributing factor caused the mishap, and it
could only be reproduced when all of the modelling inaccuracies with uncertainty variations were
incorporated**\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].

The second flight, on 27 March 2004, separated at Mach 6.946 and 94,069 feet, was fuelled for about
11 seconds and accelerated under scramjet power to a maximum of Mach
6.83\[[Marshall et al. 2005a][research_marshall_corpening_2005]\]. The third flight, on 16 November
2004, separated at Mach 9.736 and 109,440 feet against a target of Mach 9.6, was fuelled for about 10
seconds, and held thrust equal to drag at a maximum powered Mach number of
9.68\[[Marshall et al. 2005b][research_marshall_2005]\]. The programme's technology summary gives the
powered portions as 11 seconds each at about 980 and 930 pounds per square foot, and engine thrust
within less than two percent of prediction at Mach 7 and in agreement with it at Mach
10\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\]. Over the second flight's cowl-closed descent
the axial force was 10 to 15 percent higher than predicted\[[Marl and White 2006][research_davis_white_2006]\].
The Mach 10 vehicle had carbon-carbon vertical tail leading edges and a hafnium carbide coated nose
redesigned to a 0.050 inch radius, against 0.030 inch on the Mach 7
vehicles\[[Ohlhorst et al. 2005][research_ohlhorst_2005]\].

### Verified by Independent Derivation

**Every input below is a published value and every output was computed in this article.** The
qualification is made once here and not repeated against each item.

The stagnation temperatures of 2,329 and 4,588 kelvin at the two flight conditions follow from the
isentropic relation with the standard atmosphere at the stated altitudes, and the corresponding static
temperatures after deceleration to sonic conditions are 1,941 and 3,824 kelvin.

**The standard-atmosphere dynamic pressures at the two flight conditions are 955 and 973 pounds per
square foot**, within five percent of the 1,000 pound design point, against reported values of about
980 and 930. The standard atmosphere is 2.6 percent low on the second flight and 4.6 percent high on
the third.

The Kantrowitz self-starting contraction limit rises only from 1.60 to 1 at Mach 7 to 1.63 to 1 at Mach
10, which makes a fixed-geometry inlet tractable across this range.

The gain factors of 2.51, 2.00 and 1.26 correspond to the published margins of 8, 6 and under 2
decibels, and the loss of 83 percent of the available overshoot follows from them.

The interval from first anomaly to structural overload is 2.00 seconds, which at 2.5 hertz is five
cycles.

The research vehicle is 7.2 percent of stack mass and 24 percent of stack length.

Leading edge stagnation heating at the 0.030 inch design nose radius is 8.06 and 16.86 megawatts per
square metre at the two conditions, a ratio of 2.09, computed from the Sutton and Graves correlation,
and the third vehicle's 0.050 inch nose brings the ratio to 1.62.

Powered flight of 11 and 10.5 seconds covers 22.6 kilometres on the second flight and 31.1 on the
third, 6.3 and 3.5 percent short of the 15 and 20 miles reported.

The stoichiometric hydrogen to air mass ratio is 0.0292, and the 83 percent loss of gain margin
overshoot is the ratio of 1.253 to 1.512.

A net axial force of 30 to 150 pounds corresponds to accelerations of 0.01 to 0.05 g on a 3,000 pound
vehicle.

### Analysis

**These are engineering conclusions drawn in this article from the relations shown.**

Supersonic combustion is required at the upper end of this range because subsonic-combustion inlet
conditions place the air near or above dissociation before fuel is added, so the alternative destroys
the working fluid rather than merely wasting energy.

A near-constant dynamic pressure corridor follows from the competition between capture mass flow, which
wants density, and structural and thermal load, which limits it.

The thrust-drag margin is a small difference between large numbers, so ground testing and computation
cannot settle its sign when their uncertainty bands are comparable to the difference.

**The gain margin failure and the thrust-drag closure are the same epistemic problem.** Both are small
differences between large quantities, both were predicted and neither had been measured, and the programme's
value lies in having measured one of them.

Leading edge heating roughly doubles between the two flight conditions at dynamic pressures within
five percent of each other, because velocity enters cubed and density under a square root.

**Assumptions stated in the text and not taken from any source.** The five percent exit velocity
excess used to illustrate specific thrust. The one metre combustor length and the combustor velocity of
half the flight speed in the residence time estimate. The representative shock angles of 12, 15 and 20
degrees in the forebody table. The amplitude growth factors of 5, 10 and 20 in the damping table, and
the error fractions in the margin table. The separation of about 20,000 feet between the altitudes at
which the first and later stacks pass a given Mach number, in the dynamic pressure ratio of 2.48. The
standard atmosphere in place of the day's atmosphere for every flight-condition figure computed here.

### Inference

**These are reasoned conclusions the record permits but does not state.**

**The carrier aircraft weight limit is a proximate cause of the first flight's loss.** The board states
that the trajectory was chosen for B-52 weight limits and that the control system was deficient for the
trajectory flown, and NASA's history traces the weight limit to the low
launch\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\]\[[Peebles 2007][research_peebles_2007]\]. Joining those
statements into a cause is an inference this article makes and neither source makes in those words.

**The reported burn durations differ by source and by up to a second.** The technology summary gives
11 seconds of powered flight on each flight and also 10.5 seconds for the third, the flight overviews
give about 11 and about 10 seconds of fuelling, and NASA's history gives about 10 and about
11\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\]\[[Marshall et al. 2005a][research_marshall_corpening_2005]\]\[[Marshall et al. 2005b][research_marshall_2005]\]\[[Peebles 2007][research_peebles_2007]\].
The difference reflects what each counts as the burn and does not affect any conclusion here.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**The measured value of net thrust is not reconstructed in this article.** The flight established the
sign and the programme's own reconstruction established magnitudes, but reproducing those magnitudes
requires the force accounting the flight papers perform and this article does not repeat.

**Whether the corrected launch vehicle models would have been adequate for a different trajectory is
not established.** The board addressed the trajectory flown\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].

**No nomenclature reference for the X-43 designation was located**, so the statement
that the pairing is undisputed rests on the uniform usage of every source consulted and on no
register. **Uniform usage is weaker evidence than it looks**, so the gap is recorded here.

**The distances the technology summary reports are not fully reconciled.** Its 15 miles in 11 seconds
and 20 miles in 10.5 seconds\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\] imply mean speeds above the standard-atmosphere speeds at the peak powered
Mach numbers, and the summary does not say how the distances were measured.

**How much thrust margin remained above cruise at Mach 9.68 is not established**, because the planned
Mach 10 acceleration flight was never flown\[[Freeman et al. 1997][research_freeman_1997]\]\[[Peebles 2007][research_peebles_2007]\].

### On Information Postdating the Editorial Date

This article is written from current knowledge, and the contemporary survey above includes work
published after the editorial date because this series surveys the current
literature rather than reconstructing what was knowable in 2025.

## Out of Scope

**The National Aero-Space Plane** is treated only as the programme whose cancellation set the
conditions for this one. Its propulsion work, its politics and its cost are not covered.

**The X-51A Waverider** is named as the successor and treated in its own article later in this series.

**Hydrocarbon scramjet fuels** are outside this article, which treats a hydrogen vehicle. The
endothermic fuel cooling that a hydrocarbon engine requires is a different design problem.

**Detailed combustor chemistry** is taken as given. Ignition delay, mixing and flameholding are named
where they bear on the argument and are not developed.

**The force accounting methodology** used to reconstruct installed thrust from flight data is not
reproduced, although it is the technical heart of the programme's reporting.

**Hypersonic weapons policy** is out of scope entirely.

## Conclusion

**The X-43A was built to find out whether a number was positive, and it found out twice.**

The number is the difference between the thrust an airframe-integrated scramjet produces and the drag
the airframe suffers, and before 27 March 2004 nobody knew its sign in free flight, because both terms
are large, the difference is small, and the uncertainty on each term was comparable to the difference.
**The second flight accelerated and the third held speed**, which places the margin at positive at Mach
7 and at zero by design at Mach 9.68. **The pair is more useful than a speed record**,
because it shows the closure holding at both ends of the range, with thrust within two percent of
prediction and drag the larger source of error\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\].

**The first flight was destroyed by the same kind of number and the programme's own investigation said
so plainly.** A roll axis gain margin predicted at 8 decibels against a requirement of 6 became under 2
decibels once the models were corrected, and remained nominally stable even then. **The mishap
reproduced only when every modelling inaccuracy was combined with its uncertainty.** The cause lay in
the models and in no failed part, and no single error was large enough to matter. Those two facts make
the case worth recording\[[X-43A Mishap Investigation Board 2003][research_mib_2003]\].
**A margin is not a quantity. It is a quantity with an uncertainty, and this one had an uncertainty larger than itself.**

**The programme's stated product was calibrated tools rather than a vehicle**, and by that measure it
succeeded, since engine thrust came in close to prediction on both powered flights and the flights produced
a large database for the design of such vehicles\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\]. **The vehicle led nowhere directly.** The X-43C and X-43B were
still listed as planned demonstrators in the programme's 2011 retrospective\[[Grindle 2011][research_grindle_2011]\], and about eleven seconds of powered
flight at Mach 7 and ten and a half at Mach 9.68 remain the extent of what this configuration did under power\[[Voland et al. 2005][research_voland_2005]\].

**What survives is a calibration and a caution, and the caution may outlast the calibration.** The
engine data applies to hydrogen scramjets at Mach 7 and 10.
**The finding that a positive margin with an uncertainty larger than itself is indistinguishable from a negative one holds everywhere.**
